nameStory: The smallmouth flounder gets its name from its distinctively small mouth compared to other flatfish species. While most flounders have relatively large mouths for capturing prey, this little sand-dweller evolved with a tiny mouth perfectly sized for picking small morsels from the seafloor.
description: The smallmouth flounder is a tiny, flat fish that spends its life lying on sandy ocean bottoms with both eyes on one side of its head. Like all flounders, it's a master of camouflage that can change colors to match the sand beneath it. This is one of New England's smallest flatfish, rarely growing longer than a few inches, making it easy to overlook as it lies motionless on the seafloor.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Extremely small mouth that barely extends past the front edge of the lower eye - you might need to look closely to even see it

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval, flattened body that feels smooth and slippery to the touch, with both eyes positioned on the left side of the head

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small for a flatfish - typically fits easily in the palm of your hand and weighs almost nothing

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Sandy brown or grayish color that can shift slightly to match the bottom, with a pale white underside

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Continuous fins running around most of the body edge, feeling delicate and paper-thin when touched

habitat: Lives on sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters and estuaries along New England's coast. You're most likely to encounter one buried in soft sand in protected bays, harbors, or the calmer waters near river mouths where fine sediments settle.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active in warming waters and may be found in slightly shallower areas as they begin feeding more actively.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're easiest to spot moving across sandy bottoms, though still well-camouflaged.
seasonality.fall: Remains active but may move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find, often buried deeper in sand in deeper, more stable temperature waters.

funFact: Despite having two eyes on one side of its head, smallmouth flounders are actually born with normal fish anatomy - one eye on each side - but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across their skull to join the other!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young winter flounders, but the smallmouth's tiny mouth is the giveaway - if the mouth extends well past the eye, it's probably a winter flounder. Remember: 'small mouth, small flounder.'
contextualKnowledge: The smallmouth flounder belongs to the sand whiff family, which despite the unusual name simply refers to small, delicate flounders that seem to 'whiff' away like sand when disturbed.
compareHints: Since it's the only member of its genus in New England waters, compare it to other small flounders like the winter flounder. The smallmouth is distinguished by its much smaller mouth and more delicate build. While winter flounders have mouths that extend past their eyes and grow much larger, smallmouth flounders stay tiny with that characteristic pinhole mouth.
